description.text:
Japanese promotional cards with no collection number, from the first Pokémon promos of October 1996 to 2010. Bulbapedia calls them Unnumbered Promotional cards: unlike English miscellaneous promos, which are mostly reprints of expansion cards, they are often cards of their own, made for events elsewhere in the Pokémon world, and before the PROMO symbol and collection numbers arrived in mid-2001 many carried symbols and stamps of their own.

They came with guidebooks, magazines, music CDs, videos and film pamphlets, through campaigns with Toyota, All Nippon Airways and the Nintendo 64, at Pokémon Card Fan Club and World Hobby Fair events, and as prizes. Official tournaments from 1997 on, such as the Lizardon and Kamex Mega Battles, gave No.1 to No.3 Trainer cards to their top three players, and illustration, photo and card design contests had prize cards of their own. In the Diamond & Pearl years came Battle Road, Gym Challenge and World Championships cards, ending with the jumbo cards of the Clash at the Summit release campaign in 2010. Made for small events in small numbers, some of these cards are among the rarest in the game.

description.text:
One of the five "Masaki promos", from Media Factory's Evolution Communication Campaign. Vending Series 3, the vending machine sheets released from 24 November 1998, included a pass card called Bill's PC (Masaki's PC in Japanese, Masaki being Bill's Japanese name). Mailing it to Media Factory with any Kadabra card brought back this cosmos holo Alakazam, a nod to the Game Boy games, where Kadabra evolves only when traded. Haunter, Graveler, Machoke and Omanyte brought back Gengar, Golem, Machamp and Omastar the same way.

The campaign closed on 30 April 1999. Media Factory later reported in Trainers Magazine Vol. 2 that over 140,000 people took part and that 39,000 Alakazam were sent out, the most of the five. The cards came back held by their corners in a card mount printed with a thank-you letter, so many have dented corners.

description.text:
The prize of Battle Road Stadium DP, the main tournament of the Pokémon Diamond & Pearl Battle Festa★2006. The Festa replaced Battle Road's autumn season that year to celebrate the new Diamond & Pearl games and card series. It visited four venues between 25 November and 17 December 2006: Kobe International Exhibition Hall, Port Messe Nagoya, the West Japan General Exhibition Center and Pacifico Yokohama. Players brought 30-card decks. They had to win two battles in a row, then three more, to reach a Pokémon Card Laboratory researcher, one of the game's designers. Anyone who beat the researcher won this cosmos holo Stadium card, and every entrant got a Manaphy promo.

Its Japanese name, バトルロードスタジアム (Battle Road Stadium), comes from the card first given at Battle Road Autumn 2005, which used the same stage-by-stage format. This version has new Diamond & Pearl art by Ryo Ueda, with Dialga and Palkia facing each other in the arena. At the end of each player's turn, a player with 8 or more cards in hand discards down to 7.

description.text:
One of the five "Masaki promos", from Media Factory's Evolution Communication Campaign. Vending Series 3, the vending machine sheets released from 24 November 1998, included a pass card called Bill's PC (Masaki's PC in Japanese, Masaki being Bill's Japanese name). Mailing it to Media Factory with any Machoke card brought back this cosmos holo Machamp, a nod to the Game Boy games, where Machoke evolves only when traded. Kadabra, Haunter, Graveler and Omanyte brought back Alakazam, Gengar, Golem and Omastar the same way.

The campaign closed on 30 April 1999. Media Factory later reported in Trainers Magazine Vol. 2 that over 140,000 people took part and that 29,000 Machamp were sent out, the third most of the five. The cards came back held by their corners in a card mount printed with a thank-you letter, so many have dented corners.

Those who passed the hardest, the Hyper Professor Exam in the December 1998 issues, were sent this card. The magazines promised only 1,000 places, and 6th graders alone had 198 passes from 21,684 entrants. Magikarp was the university's mascot, standing for growth through study, and the campaign's Magikarp for the Game Boy games knew Dragon Rage, a move it couldn't otherwise learn; this card has Dragon Rage too, and its Pokédex text says dragon DNA has been found in Magikarp's body.

description.text:
The champion's trophy card of Battle Road Spring 2002, nine tournaments at seven venues from Tokyo on 9 March to Sapporo on 7 April 2002. It was the first year Japan's regional circuit was open to all ages, with a new masters league for players 16 and over beside the junior and senior ones, and the last in which winners got cards printed with their name: from 2003 they received the unnamed Victory Ring and Victory Orb instead.

Ken Sugimori's trainer art moved into the new e-Card frame, in a boy's and a girl's version; this is the boy's, with Growlithe, Pikachu, Chansey, Doduo, Voltorb and Marill. The winner's name, tournament, league and place were printed above the picture. Its e-Reader dot code holds a message from Imakuni? for the winner, different for each place (and, for the champions at least, for boys and girls). For the boy champion it congratulates him on his victory and signs off "Champion!". Winners were handed a dark blue folio with a certificate on stage; it was taken back afterwards and mailed with the personalized card in May 2002. The winners' list in Trainers magazine shows that 25 or 26 of the 27 champions were boys (one masters winner's name doesn't show which).

description.text:
One of the five "Masaki promos", from Media Factory's Evolution Communication Campaign. Vending Series 3, the vending machine sheets released from 24 November 1998, included a pass card called Bill's PC (Masaki's PC in Japanese, Masaki being Bill's Japanese name). Mailing it to Media Factory with any Omanyte card brought back this cosmos holo Omastar. Omanyte is the only one of the five that doesn't evolve by trading in the Game Boy games. Kadabra, Haunter, Graveler and Machoke brought back Alakazam, Gengar, Golem and Machamp the same way.

The campaign closed on 30 April 1999. Media Factory later reported in Trainers Magazine Vol. 2 that over 140,000 people took part and that 21,000 Omastar were sent out, the fewest of the five. The cards came back held by their corners in a card mount printed with a thank-you letter, so many have dented corners.

description.text:
The prize of CoroCoro Comic's first three Pokémon illustration contests, run from late 1997 to summer 1998. Headed ILLUSTRATOR where a trainer card says TRAINER, its text tells the holder that their illustration was judged excellent in the Pokémon Card Game illustration contest, and names them an officially recognized Pokémon Card illustrator. Atsuko Nishida drew its Pikachu, holding a pen.

The first contest, announced in the November 1997 issue, asked readers to draw their favorite Pokémon. Its 3 grand prize and 20 special award winners, named in the January 1998 issue, each got this card, and the three grand prize drawings were printed as cards in the first vending machine series. Two more contests in 1998, for the first film Mewtwo Strikes Back and its short Pikachu's Summer Vacation, asked entrants to design a whole card, and gave this card to eight winners each: 39 copies in all. Two further copies have since come from one of the people who wrote the game's original rules, so 41 are known.

description.text:
Never handed out: Creatures' card development team made this card and its partner Jii-kun of Tsunekazu Ishihara's two dogs as a birthday present for him in 2009. Ishihara, who founded Creatures and heads The Pokémon Company, was born on 27 November 1957, and both cards carry the date 2009.11.27. He showed them on his family blog on 26 November 2009, thanking the team and saying they were very strong combined with the previous year's present, the card "Ishihara's Trump Card" (イシハラの奥の手). They are photo cards in the frame of the HeartGold & SoulSilver era's Prime cards, credited to Creatures Inc., and collectors only learned of them in February 2023, from that blog post.

Pokey (ポキィ), the black dog, is a Darkness Pokémon with 90 HP. Its attack, Pokey's Howl, fails unless the player using it is "Mr. Ishihara", and its flavour text says its mouth is always wet, so your trousers get wet after it plays.

A photo taken in Pokémon Snap, which came out on the Nintendo 64 in Japan on 21 March 1999. description.text: From the release campaign for the Clash at the Summit expansion in 2010, when anyone who bought two of its booster packs could get this jumbo card; the campaign shared the summer with the film Zoroark: Master of Illusions, which opened in Japan on 10 July 2010. Kagemaru Himeno drew Zorua with Celebi, both of the film's cast. Its one attack, Which Is Which?, has both players swap seats and play on with the cards their opponent was using. The campaign's other card was Zoroark and Legendary Pokémon, and this one was also printed in English as a jumbo.

description.text: A bilingual card, with Japanese and English text side by side, drawn by Dr. Ooyama: Kouichi Ooyama, a game designer of the card game, who appears as Dr. Ooyama in the Game Boy game Pokémon Card GB and draws himself in the card's corner. It was first given, printed matte, to every player on the second day of the 1999 International Tropical Mega Battle in Hawaii, a US-Japan junior event, and came again glossy with the magazine Pokémon Card Trainers Vol. 3 in October 1999, which its bottom edge names. Its one attack is Stomp.

tell.text: No foil anywhere on the card.

description.text: The original matte print of this bilingual Exeggutor, given to every participant on the second day of the 1999 International Tropical Mega Battle at the Hilton Hawaiian Village (24 to 27 August 1999), the US-Japan junior event Pokumon calls the first of what became the World Championships. A glossy reprint later came in Trainer Magazine Vol. 3, so the matte original is much rarer; Dr. Ooyama's tie also reaches slightly further on it.

tell.text: No foil, but a glossy coat that looks a little shiny when held to the light.
